title: Inferences: what the passage implies
blurb: Read between the lines: combine clues from across a passage with reasoning to find what it most strongly implies.
question: A two-paragraph passage says a new graduate reread his acceptance letter, ironed his scrubs twice and left forty minutes early for a ten-minute drive. The HESI A2 asks, 'What can be inferred from the passage?' One option repeats that he left early; another says he dislikes driving. What is the correct inference, and why are those two options wrong?

teach.body: Formally, an inference is a logical conclusion based on evidence in the text plus reasoning, rather than something stated directly. In plain English: the passage gives you the clues, you connect them, and the best inference is the one the clues most strongly support, not just one that could be true. On the HESI A2 the clues are often spread across two or more paragraphs of a 250-500 word passage.

(1) Leon set his backpack by the door before his alarm went off. He reread the acceptance letter taped to the refrigerator, ironed his new navy scrubs a second time and checked twice that his badge was clipped to the pocket.

(2) The hospital was a ten-minute drive away, but he left forty minutes early. In the parking garage he sat in his car, quietly practicing the names of the unit's charge nurses, before walking to the entrance.

No sentence says 'Leon is nervous and eager about his first day,' yet every clue in both paragraphs points to it.

head: Clue type
Example from the passage
rows: Ironed the scrubs a second time
The acceptance letter on the fridge
Ten-minute drive, left forty minutes early
teach.caption: Tone, examples and cause-effect signals (because, so, as a result) are clues too.

rows.label: Example
values: He is eager about the new job

teach.body: Inference items use signal words: 'What can be inferred from paragraph 2?', 'The passage implies that...', 'The passage suggests...', 'Which statement is most strongly supported?'. Many ask why, not what: why the author included a detail, what a phrase suggests, who the intended reader is. A leaflet that speaks to 'you' and says 'bring this card to every visit' was written for patients, even though it never says so. Answer from the clues, never from what you happen to know about the topic.

items: Spot the signal in the stem: infer, imply, suggest, most likely, most strongly supported.
If the stem names a paragraph, reread that paragraph first; otherwise skim each paragraph's gist.
Ask: given these lines, what must be true or is most strongly supported?
Eliminate options that are stated outright, extreme (always, never, all), based on outside knowledge or unsupported.
Choose the option that every relevant detail supports and no paragraph contradicts.

teach.h: How strongly does the text support it?
teach.caption: The correct answer sits at the top of this scale. 'Could be true' is level 2, and it is a trap.

teach.text: Four inference traps: (1) an option that is directly stated, which is locating, not inferring; (2) an extreme option with all, never, always or proves; (3) an option that relies on outside knowledge or personal opinion; (4) reversed cause and effect. In a longer passage, also watch for an option that fits one paragraph but clashes with another.

teach.body: Keisha Morgan, applying to a practical nursing program, reads a two-paragraph clinic memo. Paragraph 1 says flu shots will be given in Room 4 only, starting Monday. Paragraph 2 says, 'Please direct walk-in patients there and remind them to bring their insurance card.' Asked what can be inferred about the audience, she notices that the readers are told to direct patients: the memo is for front-desk staff, not patients. Nothing says 'to staff', but the clues require it.

items: Inference = evidence in the text + reasoning; not stated directly.
The best inference is the most strongly supported one, not merely a possible one.
Clues can sit in different paragraphs: check the whole passage before you choose.
Inference items also ask about purpose, the meaning of a phrase and the intended audience.
Reject stated facts, extreme words, outside knowledge and reversed cause and effect.

summary: You can now draw inferences by connecting clues from across a passage with reasoning, including inferences about an author's purpose, a phrase's meaning and the intended audience. You can rank options by strength of support and reject stated, extreme, outside-knowledge and reversed options.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) The waiting room clock read 4:52. Mr. Okafor had already paged through every magazine on the table twice, and he looked up each time the door to the exam rooms opened. Twice he walked to the window, glanced at the parking lot and sat back down.

(2) When a nurse finally called his name, he stood so quickly that his chair scraped the floor. He gathered his coat and folder and was through the door before she had finished saying the room number.

Which statement about Mr. Okafor can be inferred from the passage?
options: He arrived late and missed the time of his original appointment.
He is angry at the receptionist for calling other patients first.
He has been waiting a long time and is eager to be seen.
He has to wait longer than other patients at every visit.
A.why: Reading every magazine twice, watching the door, pacing to the window and jumping up when called all point to a long wait and eagerness to be seen. Every clue in both paragraphs supports it, and none contradicts it.

whyNot.0: The passage does not mention when he arrived or what time his appointment was.
whyNot.1: Overreach: impatience is supported, but the passage gives no sign of anger at the receptionist.
whyNot.3: Extreme: the passage describes one visit and cannot support a claim about every visit.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Bring this card to every visit. Write down any new medicine you start, including vitamins and herbal products, and cross out any medicine you stop. Note the dose and how often you take it.

(2) If you see more than one doctor, show this card to each of them, even if you think they already know what you take. Pharmacists can also review the card when you pick up a new prescription. Keep the card in your wallet so that it is with you in an emergency.

It can be inferred that the card is mainly meant to:
options: warn patients that herbal products interfere with medicines
persuade patients to see a single doctor for all of their care
help patients keep each provider aware of everything they take
explain to doctors how to record the vitamins a patient takes
A.why: Every instruction (list everything including vitamins, cross out stopped medicines, show it to each doctor and the pharmacist, carry it in an emergency) serves one purpose: making sure every provider knows everything the patient takes.

whyNot.0: Herbal products are listed as things to record; the passage does not say they interfere with anything.
whyNot.1: The passage assumes patients may see more than one doctor and tells them what to do; it does not argue against it.
whyNot.3: The card is addressed to patients ('you'), not doctors.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) When the new office manager arrived, the old routines were swept out with the dust. On her first morning, staff who had used the same paper forms for twenty years were handed tablets, and the weekly meeting moved from Friday afternoons to Monday mornings.

(2) By the end of her first week, the filing cabinets that had lined the hallway were gone, and a whiteboard listing each day's appointments hung in their place.

The phrase 'swept out with the dust' in paragraph 1 suggests that the old routines were:
options: quickly removed as outdated
cleaned up and kept in use
slowly phased out over years
stored with the old paper forms
A.why: Dust is something old and unwanted that is cleared away. The details (tablets on the first morning, the meeting moved, the cabinets gone within a week) show the change was fast. So the routines were removed quickly as outdated.

whyNot.1: Sweeping something out means getting rid of it, not keeping it.
whyNot.2: The changes happened in her first morning and first week, not over years.
whyNot.3: This reads the phrase literally; the passage does not say the routines were stored anywhere.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Marisol has worked night shifts at the care home for six years. She keeps a spare pair of shoes in her locker, knows which residents like the radio on at 3 a.m., and can tell from footsteps in the hall which resident is up and wandering.

(2) New staff are told on their first night that if something goes wrong and they are unsure what to do, they should find Marisol. Last winter, when the power failed during a storm, she had flashlights handed out before the backup generator started.

Which of the following is an inference rather than a stated fact?
options: Marisol has worked night shifts at the care home for six years.
Marisol keeps a spare pair of shoes in her locker at the home.
Marisol prefers night shifts to day shifts at the care home.
Coworkers regard Marisol as experienced and dependable.
B.why: No sentence says coworkers see Marisol as dependable, but new staff being told to find her when something goes wrong, plus her six years, her detailed knowledge and her quick action in the storm, strongly support it.

whyNot.0: This is stated directly in paragraph 1, so it is a fact from the text, not an inference.
whyNot.1: This is stated directly in paragraph 1.
whyNot.2: Unsupported: working nights for six years does not show she prefers them; the passage does not compare shifts.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) In the first week of the hospital's new badge system, a line of about 20 people formed at the east entrance every morning at 7:00, when the day shift arrives. Each person had to hold a badge to the reader and wait for a green light before the door unlocked.

(2) The west entrance, used mostly by visitors after 10:00, had no line at any time. In the second week, the hospital added a second badge reader at the east entrance, and the morning line disappeared.

What can be inferred about the cause of the morning line?
options: Many staff arriving at one entrance at once caused the line.
The badge readers at the east entrance were not working properly.
Visitors avoided the new badge system by using the west entrance.
Visitors slowly learning the badge system caused the east line.
B.why: The line appeared at the time and place where the day shift arrives, nowhere else, and it vanished once a second reader was added. Those clues point to many staff badging in at one door at once.

whyNot.1: The passage reports no fault; adding a second reader fixed the line, which points to too few readers, not broken ones.
whyNot.2: Visitors use the west entrance after 10:00; the passage does not suggest they were avoiding the system.
whyNot.3: Visitors mostly use the west entrance after 10:00; the east line formed at 7:00, when the day shift arrives.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Keep this sheet on your refrigerator. If your child's temperature reaches 100.4°F or higher, call our nurse line before giving a second dose of fever reducer. Do not give adult tablets to a child, even if you cut them in half.

(2) Use the measuring cup that comes with liquid medicine, not a kitchen spoon. Write down the time of each dose so that everyone who cares for your child knows when the last one was given. Our nurse line is open 24 hours a day.

What can be inferred about the intended audience of the sheet?
options: Nurses who answer the clinic's nurse line
Pharmacists who prepare children's medicine
Older children who take their own medicine
Parents or caregivers of young patients
B.why: The sheet speaks to 'you' about 'your child', tells the reader to call the nurse line, to keep the sheet at home and to log doses for everyone who cares for the child. Those clues point to parents or caregivers.

whyNot.0: The reader is told to call the nurse line, so the reader is not the nurse who answers it.
whyNot.1: Advice to keep the sheet on the refrigerator and log doses at home is aimed at home care, not pharmacy work.
whyNot.2: The sheet refers to 'your child', so it addresses an adult responsible for a child.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Dr. Lena Ortiz spent the summer testing water from 40 private wells across Harlan County. She found that 9 of them contained nitrate levels above the federal limit, most of them near large farms.

(2) In her report, Dr. Ortiz notes that she grew up drinking water from one of those wells. She sent each family a letter explaining its results and offered to return in the fall to test again at no cost.

What can be inferred about why the author mentions, in paragraph 2, where Dr. Ortiz grew up?
options: To prove the wells were safe during Dr. Ortiz's childhood
To suggest that Dr. Ortiz has a personal stake in the results
To explain why Dr. Ortiz tested 40 wells and not more of them
To show that Dr. Ortiz was not qualified to test the wells
C.why: Placing her childhood well among those tested signals a personal connection to the findings, and her letters to each family and free follow-up testing fit that connection. That is the most strongly supported reason for including the detail.

whyNot.0: The passage says nothing about water quality during her childhood.
whyNot.2: Where she grew up has no stated link to the number of wells tested.
whyNot.3: The passage does not question her qualifications; a personal connection does not imply a lack of skill.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) For years, Brookside Clinic closed at 5 p.m., and about one in five scheduled appointments ended as a no-show. Reminder calls, text messages and a printed schedule on every discharge sheet did little to change that number.

(2) After the clinic began offering appointments until 8 p.m., the number of missed appointments fell by about a third. Most of the new evening slots were booked by patients who work daytime jobs.

Which inference is best supported by the passage?
options: Missed appointments led the clinic to end its daytime hours.
Patients with daytime jobs seldom miss evening appointments.
Evening appointments cost the clinic less than daytime ones.
Daytime jobs had kept some patients from attending.
C.why: Reminders did not reduce no-shows, but adding evening hours did, and working patients took most of the new slots. The best-supported inference is that daytime jobs had been keeping some patients from their appointments.

whyNot.0: Distortion: the clinic added evening hours; the passage does not say daytime hours ended.
whyNot.1: Overreach: the passage reports a drop in missed visits overall, not the attendance record of working patients in particular.
whyNot.2: Costs are not mentioned, so this has no support in the text.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) The sign on the community pool's gate read 'Closed for repairs until further notice.' Behind the fence, the pool held no water, and two workers knelt on its floor, patching long cracks with gray cement.

(2) A stack of new tiles sat beside the diving board, and a hose ran from a pump at the deep end to a drain in the parking lot. A child pressed her face to the fence and asked her father whether they could swim tomorrow; he pointed to the sign and shook his head.

Which statement can be inferred from the passage?
options: The pool was drained so its floor could be repaired.
The pool will reopen to swimmers within the next week.
The pool closed after a swimmer was injured on a crack.
The diving board is being replaced with a set of tiles.
C.why: An empty pool, a pump hose running to a drain, workers patching cracks on the floor and a 'closed for repairs' sign together strongly support that the pool was drained for floor repairs.

whyNot.1: Possible but unsupported: the sign says 'until further notice', and the father's answer suggests no quick reopening.
whyNot.2: No injury is mentioned; this invents a cause the text does not give.
whyNot.3: Distortion: the tiles sit beside the diving board; the passage does not say they replace it.

reteach.title: Think like a detective
reteach.question: A detective finds muddy boot prints leading from the back door to the kitchen and an open, empty cookie jar. How is the detective's thinking like answering a HESI A2 inference question?

blocks.body: A good detective does not say 'the butler did it' because butlers often do (outside knowledge). Nor does she say 'someone came in the back door' and stop, because that is simply what the prints show (stated). She reasons: muddy prints from outside, straight to an empty jar, means someone came in from outside and took the cookies. That conclusion uses every clue and contradicts none. HESI A2 inferences work the same way.

steps.label: Clue
steps.sub: Muddy prints from the back door

steps.label: Clue
steps.sub: Empty cookie jar in the kitchen

steps.label: Reasoning
steps.sub: Prints lead straight to the jar

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.sub: Someone came in and took the cookies

blocks.text: 'It could be true' is not enough. A detective who accuses someone with no clues pointing to them gets the case thrown out.

explain.body: An inference is a conclusion reached by combining evidence in the text with reasoning. It is not written in the text, but the text must support it.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) By noon on Thursday, the grocery store's shelves of bottled water, batteries and bread were nearly bare, and the parking lot was full. Several shoppers pushed carts loaded with canned soup and candles.

(2) A radio near the checkout was tuned to a weather station, and a worker taped a handwritten sign to the door: 'Flashlights sold out. More expected Monday.'

What can be inferred from the passage?
options: The store had forgotten to order enough water and bread that week.
Shoppers were preparing for a storm that had been forecast.
The store sells more batteries than any other product it stocks.
The radio station had told listeners to shop at that store.
test.why: Water, batteries, bread and flashlights selling out, carts of soup and candles, and a radio on a weather station together point to people stocking up before forecast bad weather.

whyNot.0: The passage gives no sign of an ordering problem; a full parking lot points to high demand.
whyNot.2: Overreach: the passage describes one morning, not overall sales.
whyNot.3: The passage does not say the station mentioned this store.

explain.body: Clues come from actions, details included or left out, word choice and tone. A person's actions often reveal a feeling the text never names, and the clues may be spread across paragraphs.

head: Clue
Suggests
rows: Checks the clock again and again

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Tomas had not slept well since the biopsy. When the envelope from the lab finally arrived, he read the results twice, folded the paper carefully and let out a long breath.

(2) Then he called his sister. She could hear him laughing before he had even said hello, and he told her she could cancel the extra shifts she had offered to cover for him.

What can be inferred about the results?
options: They were worse than Tomas had expected.
They were confusing and hard to read.
They were a relief to Tomas.
They were meant for his sister.
test.why: Sleepless worry, then a long breath out, laughing and telling his sister she no longer needs to cover his shifts, all signal relief: the results were good news to him.

whyNot.0: Laughing and canceling the extra help do not fit bad news.
whyNot.1: Reading twice could suggest care, but his relieved reaction does not fit confusion.
whyNot.3: He told his sister the news; the passage does not say the results were hers.

explain.body: Inference items also ask why a detail is included, what a phrase suggests or who the reader is. Look at what the detail does in context: does it build trust, give an example, show contrast?

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) The article on safe lifting at work quotes Ray Delgado, who spent 25 years as a warehouse supervisor before training as a physical therapist. Delgado says most of the back injuries he has seen came from twisting while lifting, not from the weight of the load itself.

(2) He recommends turning the whole body by moving the feet, keeping the load close to the waist and asking for help with anything awkward to carry.

What can be inferred about why the author includes Delgado's background?
options: To show that warehouse work is more dangerous than therapy
To explain why Delgado decided to leave the warehouse
To suggest that Delgado's advice comes from experience
To argue that supervisors should train as therapists
test.why: Twenty-five years supervising lifting plus therapy training tells readers his advice is grounded in experience, which makes his claims and recommendations more credible.

whyNot.0: The passage does not compare the danger of the two jobs.
whyNot.1: His reasons for changing careers are not discussed.
whyNot.3: No recommendation about supervisors is made or implied.

explain.body: Several options may be possible. Choose the one the details require or most strongly support, and reject anything extreme, unsupported or reversed.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) The bakery's display case was full when the doors opened at 7 a.m., with six trays of blueberry muffins and six trays of bran muffins, all at the same price.

(2) By 9 a.m., every blueberry muffin was gone, and two customers had asked whether more were coming. Every tray of bran muffins was still full.

What can be inferred from the passage?
options: Customers that morning preferred blueberry to bran.
The bakery will stop baking bran muffins later this month.
Bran muffins cost more at this bakery than blueberry ones.
Blueberry muffins are the best-selling item at every bakery.
test.why: With equal numbers on offer at the same price, one kind sold out and drew requests for more while the other did not sell in the same two hours. Customers that morning picked blueberry over bran.

whyNot.1: A prediction about the bakery's plans is not supported by one morning's sales.
whyNot.2: Contradicts paragraph 1, which says the muffins were all the same price.
whyNot.3: Extreme: one bakery on one morning says nothing about every bakery.
